svg.aria-label: Where each engine keeps old row versions for MVCC. PostgreSQL keeps old row versions in the table itself, marked with xmin and xmax, and VACUUM removes dead versions; long transactions cause bloat. MySQL InnoDB updates rows in place and rebuilds older versions from undo logs, which the purge thread cleans; long transactions grow the history list. Oracle updates blocks in place and rebuilds read-consistent blocks from the undo tablespace; if undo is overwritten a long query fails with ORA-01555 snapshot too old. MongoDB WiredTiger and Oak both give each reader a snapshot: WiredTiger keeps history in its cache, which is why transactions are time-limited, and an Oak session sees a repository revision until it refreshes, with conflicting saves rejected.
svg.text: MVCC everywhere, but old versions live in different places
Readers don't block writers in any of these engines. What differs is where history is kept, and what a long transaction costs you.
UPDATE writes a new row version in the
heap; the old one stays, marked dead
VACUUM removes versions no snapshot needs
Long transaction: table and index bloat
UPDATE IN PLACE, HISTORY IN UNDO
Row updated in the clustered index;
old values written to undo logs
walking the undo chain; purge cleans up
Each operation or transaction reads a point-in-time snapshot.
History needed by open snapshots is pinned in the cache.
Concurrent writes to the same document: write conflict,
Long transaction: cache pressure, so it is time-limited
A session sees one repository revision until it refreshes.
Changes are transient until save(), which commits them atomically.
A save that conflicts with a newer revision fails
Long-lived session: stale reads and conflicts
